english_translation: Today things went much better than I initially expected.

dialogue.shona: Nhasi zvinhu zvafamba zvakanaka kupfuura zvandaitarisira pakutanga.
dialogue.english: Today things went much better than I initially expected.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Nhasi [today] • zvinhu [things nhu] • zvafamba [zvafamba] • zvakanaka [well / nicely / very good] • kupfuura [to / at pfuura] • zvandaitarisira [zvandaitarisira] • pakutanga [on / at kutanga]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kupfuura')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kupfuura' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvakanaka'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Expressing Gratitude When a Day Exceeds Expectations
cultural_notes.content: Reflecting at the end of the day that 'zvinhu zvafamba zvakanaka kupfuura zvandaitarisira' ('things went even better than I expected') is a common way to share good news with family.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new polite request into English: 'Chimbomirira zvishoma pamusuwo.'
options: Come inside the house and sit on the chair.
Please wait a little while at the door.
Return home early before the sun sets.
Take your books and put them in the bag.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Chimbomirira' = 'Wait a little / for a moment right now', 'zvishoma' = 'a little', 'pamusuwo' = 'at the door'.

active_exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Mhoro' and 'Mhoroi'?
options: 'Mhoro' is used only at night, while 'Mhoroi' is used in the morning
'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
'Mhoro' is used in shops, while 'Mhoroi' is used only at school
active_exercises.correct_answer: 'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' ('Mhoro' -> 'Mhoroi') shows plural or respectful address.
